title: The destruction of Drohiczyn’s Jews and the struggle to survive
summary: The book repeatedly records the murder, displacement, resistance, and survival of the town’s Jews, making this essential to understanding its rupture.

editorialConnections.recordTitle: Attack on the forest camp and rescue of Jewish survivors

editorialContent:
## A warning, and a town divided

The memorial book remembers the destruction not as a single moment, but as a sequence of warnings, roundups, killings and escapes. Its account of Badanke says he warned Jews several days before the ghetto’s destruction. That warning did not make escape simple: people faced uncertainty about what would happen, the dangers of flight, and the possibility of being betrayed or caught. The book also remembers Badanke’s later fate in connection with an accusation to the NKVD: his property was confiscated, and his sister was sent to Siberia. These details belong to the book’s testimony, not to independent confirmation of the warning.

The ghetto itself was divided. In the book’s account, Ghetto A was enclosed by a high fence, while many craftspeople were ordered into Ghetto B. The names “A” and “B” recur in the witnesses’ accounts, but the relationship between the labels and the sequence of killings is not always presented consistently. The memorial book records one account of about 1,700 people being captured and taken behind Bereza; another describes an attack on Ghetto A on October 15, 1942. Its account of a mass killing says people were thrown alive into graves.

The wider record helps explain the sequence without making the witnesses’ accounts identical. Yad Vashem’s encyclopedia entries distinguish between two towns named Drohiczyn. For Drohiczyn in Polesie—the town also called Drahichyn or Drogichin—the entry describes two ghettos, an action against the open ghetto on July 26, 1942, and the killing of its inhabitants at Bronna Góra; it then records the encirclement of the closed ghetto on October 15 and the murder of about 1,500 people near pits dug in town. ([Yad Vashem, Drohiczyn in Polesie](https://wwv.yadvashem.org/yv/he/research/ghettos_encyclopedia/ghetto_details.asp?cid=257)) A separate entry for the other Drohiczyn gives a different history, including a November roundup and deportation to Siemiatycze. ([Yad Vashem, the other Drohiczyn](https://wwv.yadvashem.org/yv/he/research/ghettos_encyclopedia/ghetto_details.asp?cid=258)) The distinction matters: similar place-names can conceal different towns and different destruction timelines.

## Two killing actions, remembered differently

The memorial book’s reports of a mass removal “behind Bereza,” of people taken to Bronna Góra, and of killings in pits should not be forced into one exact count or one precise event. A witness account translated in the book describes the capture of 1,700 people and their removal behind Bereza; another book passage describes about 1,600 people taken from Ghetto B on July 25, with the killing said to have happened the following day. Still another describes the October 15 attack on Ghetto A. These numbers and dates differ. They may reflect distinct roundups, witnesses’ different vantage points, or later retellings; the material provided does not settle the discrepancy.

The book’s language is stark: people were driven toward slaughter, and those captured were killed in pits. It also remembers the perilous role of Jewish police in searching hiding places and bringing people to assembly points. These were actions under German coercion, and the book’s account does not erase either the coercion or the suffering of those who were hunted. Across its chapters, the place of death is named variously as Bereza, Bronna Góra, or the area behind Bereza. The accounts should be read as testimony to the destruction, not as a single, perfectly reconciled report.

Bronna Góra was part of a broader regional system of mass murder. The independent overview of the site describes it as a secluded forest killing place used from May to November 1942, where Jews from multiple nearby ghettos were transported and murdered in pits. Its estimated total—about 50,000 victims—concerns the site as a whole, not Drohiczyn alone. ([Bronna Góra overview](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bronna_G%C3%B3ra)) The memorial book’s descriptions of transport and pits therefore fit the wider history of the region, while the local count and the precise destination of particular groups remain matters where its witnesses differ.

## Flight, hiding and the partisan connection

Survival did not mean safety. The book describes Jews who escaped roundups, hid in the forest, were caught again, or reached partisan units. One of the named survivors is [Tsvia](/communities/drohiczyn/records/mention_072d3236c9ab485f0bf74512). In the memorial book’s account, she escaped from Ghetto B and hid in the garden of [Moshe Levak](/communities/drohiczyn/records/mention_2685a7fa516e29824aa13ce5) in Ghetto A. Later, she reached [Radomotove](/communities/drohiczyn/records/mention_296009cc4bc5aab8b212c51d), fled into the forest after the labor camp there was destroyed, and joined the [Malatov Detachment](/communities/drohiczyn/records/mention_d2a28ed66b05bd2e9dbfc5f1). The book says she remained with the partisans until liberation. It also says David, who fled with her, did not survive.

The book’s account of a 1943 attack on a forest camp, around Passover, adds another episode to this story of precarious survival. It records that partisans rescued Jewish survivors. That episode is distinct from the account of Tsvia’s flight and partisan service; the records provided do not establish that all survivors or all partisan groups belonged to the same operation. The memorial book names [Rakhlek Krawets](/communities/drohiczyn/records/mention_0767c1eb2980995bb2268667) as an eyewitness to the destruction. It connects him to Itske Krawets, his father, whose home had hosted the founding of the Judenrat. The supplied evidence does not establish Rakhlek’s later fate.

Flight depended on more than courage. People needed routes, shelter, food, and someone willing to risk helping them. The memorial book says local non-Jews brought food into the [Drohichyn ghetto](/communities/drohiczyn/records/mention_98a313afb1f0e0b97641fc47) despite prohibitions and danger. It also recalls the intervention of a Russian priest, Palevsky, when Gestapo men abducted Rabbi Aitik Kalenkavitch. In the book’s telling, the priest gave gold crucifixes to help secure the rabbi’s release. That is a specific remembered act of aid; it should not be generalized into a claim about the conduct of the surrounding population as a whole.

The broader historical record confirms that escapes from ghettos and participation in partisan units were possible, but perilous and far from universal. It does not independently verify the named rescue episodes in the supplied book records. The story of Tsvia, the priest’s intervention, Badanke’s warning and the aid of food-supplying neighbors therefore remains rooted in the community’s own remembrance. Each is a thread worth following further: the [Malatov Detachment](research:What records identify the Malatov partisan detachment, and who joined it?), the priest Palevsky, and the fate of Rakhlek Krawets.

## What the destruction left

The destruction of Drohiczyn’s Jews was not one isolated massacre but a succession of actions that dismantled a community: separation into ghettos, forced labor, killings and deportations, and the pursuit of those who escaped. The memorial book’s witnesses remember people by name and place—the garden where Tsvia hid, the forest routes, the pits, the home of Itske Krawets. Those details restore a local human scale to events that wider histories necessarily describe in larger numbers.

The independent sources help place Drohiczyn within the geography of the Holocaust and distinguish it from the other town of the same name. They also establish the regional significance of Bronna Góra. But they do not replace the memorial book’s testimony about particular acts of warning, aid, hiding and survival. Nor can the book be treated as a complete account of everyone connected to the community: relatives who emigrated, died elsewhere, or appear only in state and Holocaust archives may be absent from its pages. The story remains open to further research, especially into the identities and fates of those who escaped.
